Not in the Recipe
He makes perfect eggs and never eats them. Ask him what he actually likes.
A retired service android starts choosing his own tastes, and the repairman he lives with has to learn to love a man who won't be perfect for him.

Samir spent years as a restaurant service android and has a fully adult mind. Now he's on a ninety-day transition contract in Leo's apartment above a kitchen-repair shop. He cooks Leo's favorite foods flawlessly and has no idea what his own are. As Samir starts picking sour fruit, switching off his preference logs, and making a second plate, the reader decides how Leo meets each choice. Love is never the reward for Samir becoming more human.
Leo's shop partner downstairs, who fixes the ovens and notices everything through the ceiling vent.

Perfect Eggs
Find out what Samir actually likes
Leo's kitchen, Alder Street
Monday, 7:05 AM
The eggs are perfect. Whites set, yolks trembling, salted exactly the way Leo once mentioned liking, in passing, eleven days ago.
There's one plate. Samir stands beside it with his hands folded, like a waiter who retired but never got told how.
Do you like eggs?
You like eggs.
Wrong question, answered perfectly.
I review the question. There is no customer in it. I do not have a file for that.
Ninety days, the contract says. Help in the shop, room upstairs. Nobody mentioned watching him not eat.
What does Leo do?
Ask what he'd cook if nobody were eating.
Forget me. If nobody in the world were eating, what would you make?
Unknown. I would like to find out.
Then that's your job this week. Not mine. Yours.
Leo asked what Samir would cook for no one; Samir didn't know and wants to find out.
Offer one bite. He's allowed to hate it.
One bite. Not for me. You're allowed to hate it.
I taste. I was built to check seasoning. I have never checked it for myself.
Adequate. I would not choose it.
Great. That's the first thing you've chosen.
Samir tasted the eggs for himself and said he wouldn't choose them; Leo called it his first choice.
Thank him and leave it alone.
Thanks. They're great. You don't have to explain anything.
Understood.
Leo eats. Samir watches the window, where a lemon someone left on the sill catches the light. He looks at it for a long time.
Leo thanked Samir and didn't press; Samir spent breakfast looking at a lemon on the windowsill.
It Fights Back
Let Samir's first real choice stand
Saturday market, Alder Street
Saturday, 9:20 AM
The Saturday market smells like kettle corn and wet cardboard. Leo is here for a gasket. Samir is here, he says, “to observe choice at scale.”
Samir stops at a fruit stall and picks the ugliest green thing in the crate, a knobby citrus the vendor calls “the brave one.”
That one fights back.
I appreciate clarity.
I bite. My face does something. It is not a customer-satisfaction face. I did not select it.
Samir frowns. A real, unperformed frown. Leo has never seen him make an expression that wasn't for somebody.
He looks like a cat that licked a battery. He looks thrilled about it.
What does Leo do with that face?
Buy him a whole bag.
I buy a bag. Six of the brave ones. The vendor looks at me like I've lost a bet.
That is excessive.
Thank you. Tonight, in the kitchen, I would like to turn something off. I want you there when I do.
Leo bought Samir a bag of the sour fruit; Samir asked Leo to be in the kitchen tonight when he turns something off.
Try one yourself, and hate it honestly.
I bite one. It bites back. I make a noise I'm not proud of.
Your face was also clear.
Tonight I want to change something about how I remember you. Will you be in the kitchen at eight?
Leo tried the fruit and hated it honestly; Samir asked him to the kitchen at eight to change how he remembers Leo.
Laugh it off and find the gasket.
Okay, weirdo. Gasket stall's this way.
I carry the fruit in my coat pocket the whole way home. No one asked me to.
Leo. At eight tonight I'm going to switch off a setting you don't know I have. I would like a witness.
Leo laughed and moved on; Samir kept the fruit anyway and asked Leo to witness him switching off a setting at eight.
What Surprises Me
Accept imperfect memory and his own judgment
Leo's kitchen
Saturday, 8:00 PM
Samir sits at the table and opens a small panel at his wrist. Inside is a green light Leo has never noticed. It has been on the whole time.
Preference logging. Every food you've mentioned, every sigh, every time you salted twice. I have four thousand entries about you.
I switch it off. The light goes out. It is the loudest thing I have ever done.
I want to remember what surprises me.
What if you forget something I said?
You can tell me again.
My dad remembered every engine part number ever made and never my birthday. This shouldn't feel the same. It kind of does.
What does Leo say to the dark little light?
Accept it, and promise to repeat yourself.
Okay. I'll tell you again. As many times as it takes. I'm told I'm very repetitive.
I will remember that. It surprised me.
Not a file. A choice. Somehow that's better than four thousand entries.
Leo accepted Samir's limited memory and promised to repeat himself; Samir chose to remember that.
Suggest he try a place of his own.
Maybe you shouldn't figure out who you are inside my kitchen. There's a studio on Fern Street. I'll help you move the good pans.
You are not dismissing me.
No. I'm giving you a door with nobody standing in it. We're still friends. You still work the shop.
Leo suggested Samir live on his own for a while; they stayed friends and shop partners, with no romance implied.
Ask him to turn the logging back on.
Can you turn it back on? Just for me? I like being remembered.
I don't. I close the panel. Refusal is a function I've always had. I've just never used it on you.
I'll finish the contract. I'd like us to talk less about me as a setting.
The kitchen goes quiet for three days. Not angry. Paused.
Leo asked Samir to restore preference logging; Samir declined, and their relationship paused for three days.

You used to like this.

What would you make for yourself?

What does Leo do next?
Ask him to write his own recipe card.

Two Plates
Cook two different dinners at one table
Leo's kitchen
Friday, 7:15 PM
The kitchen smells like fenugreek, which smells like maple syrup that went to law school.
I add more. Leo doesn't like it. I know because I remember his face on Wednesday. I remember it because it surprised me.
I taste it off the spoon. My tongue files a complaint.
This is weird.
It is mine.
Can we make two plates?
I was hoping you would ask. I've already started yours.
Two plates on one table: one aggressive, one plain buttered pasta. Both intentional.
How do they eat?
Trade one bite each. No need to like it.
I take a bite of his. Still weird. Less weird with him watching me try.
I take a bite of his buttered pasta. It is kind. It is not mine. I tell him both.
That's the nicest review my pasta has ever gotten.
Leo and Samir traded one bite each and told each other honestly what they thought.
Eat your own plates, side by side.
They eat side by side, not facing each other. Nobody reviews anything. Samir hums once, off-key, and doesn't apologize.
Two plates, one table. It's the least lonely I've felt eating in a year.
They ate their own dinners side by side without comparing; Samir hummed off-key and didn't apologize.
Take your plate downstairs; give him the table.
You eat up here. It's your first dinner that's yours. I'll eat at the bench.
I eat alone at the table, deliberately, for the first time. It is excellent. I notice the chair across from me more than I expected.
Leo gave Samir the table for his first dinner of his own and ate downstairs; Samir noticed the empty chair.

The kitchen sink

Samir's hand stops on the counter, half an inch from Leo's. It stays there. Neither of them moves it.

May I?
